EV: Against a pipeline requirement of 2,610 at the current win rate.
The shortfall between leads produced and leads the target requires.
Up 56% across the period while volume growth flattened.

PHASES.t: Quantify the demand gap against pipeline maths
PHASES.dw: The required lead volume is calculated and the gap is a single agreed number.
PHASES.hyp: The shortfall can be stated as one number, and until it is, every argument about channels is an opinion.
PHASES.obj: A defensible figure for how many qualified leads per cycle the target requires, and how far short you are.
PHASES.why: Nothing downstream can be sized until the gap is. Channel selection without it is guesswork with a budget attached.
steps: Pull win rate and average deal value from the last four cycles.
Back-solve the qualified leads required to hit target.
Compare against actual qualified leads produced.
Agree the gap figure with sales and finance.
Publish it where both teams can see it.
PHASES.del: A one page demand gap calculation signed off by sales and finance.
PHASES.li: A single gap number that nobody disputes.
PHASES.watch: Averaging across an unrepresentative quarter. If one large deal distorts the win rate, the gap comes out flattering.

PHASES.t: Audit existing sources for unused headroom
PHASES.dw: Every current source has a stated ceiling and a cost to reach it.
PHASES.hyp: A meaningful share of the gap can be closed by scaling what already works, before anything new is built.
PHASES.obj: A ranked view of current sources by remaining headroom and marginal cost per qualified lead.
PHASES.why: New channels take a cycle to prove. Existing ones can move next week, so they are always the cheaper first move.
steps: List every source producing qualified leads today.
Establish current volume and cost per qualified lead for each.
Estimate remaining headroom before efficiency degrades.
Rank by marginal cost to add one more qualified lead.
Decide what scales now versus what is tapped out.
PHASES.del: A source ranking with headroom and marginal cost per qualified lead.
PHASES.li: Share of the gap addressable without any new channel.
PHASES.watch: Treating a channel as tapped out because spend rose without results. Check creative and offer fatigue before writing it off.

PHASES.t: Select net new channels against ICP fit
PHASES.dw: Two channels are chosen with a written rationale and a sized test budget.
PHASES.hyp: The residual gap needs channels the ICP actually uses, not the channels the market is loudest about.
PHASES.obj: A short list of net new channels scoped to the residual gap and sized against how the ICP buys.
PHASES.why: Committing budget to a channel is the expensive decision. Making it explicitly, against fit, is what keeps it recoverable.
steps: Map where the ICP already looks for solutions like yours.
Score candidate channels on fit, cost and time to signal.
Size a test budget against the residual gap only.
Define the qualification bar before any spend starts.
Commit to two channels, not five.
PHASES.del: A channel selection memo with fit rationale and sized test budgets.
PHASES.li: Channels chosen on documented fit rather than availability.
PHASES.watch: Chasing a channel because a competitor is loud on it. If it does not match how your ICP buys, it will generate cheap volume that never converts. Fit beats fashion.

PHASES.t: Stand up a repeatable demand engine with weekly output
PHASES.dw: The engine is live with a defined weekly output and at least two consecutive weeks shipped on cadence.
PHASES.hyp: The chosen channels can produce demand on a predictable weekly cadence rather than in one off bursts, and repeatability is what closes the gap sustainably.
PHASES.obj: A repeatable demand motion is live on at least one chosen channel with a committed weekly output and an owner accountable for it.
PHASES.why: A sizeable gap does not close on sporadic effort. Standing up a weekly output engine now is what turns channel selection into sustained volume instead of a spike that fades.
steps: Define the weekly output unit for the channel, posts, sequences or campaigns.
Build the production process to hit that cadence reliably.
Assign a named owner accountable for weekly output.
Launch the first two weeks of output live.
Track qualified leads produced per weekly cycle.
PHASES.del: A live demand engine on at least one channel with a committed weekly output cadence and a named owner.
PHASES.li: Qualified leads per weekly cycle rising across the first cycles of the engine.
PHASES.watch: Launching in a burst and calling it an engine. If output depends on one heroic push rather than a repeatable process, volume collapses the moment attention moves elsewhere.

PHASES.t: Protect lead quality so new volume still converts
PHASES.dw: The qualification bar is defined and enforced in your CRM and new channel conversion is reviewed weekly against baseline.
PHASES.hyp: New volume risks diluting lead quality, and without a quality guardrail the added leads will convert worse and recreate the shortage one stage down.
PHASES.obj: A qualification guardrail is in place so new channel leads convert at or near the rate of existing qualified leads, with any dilution caught weekly.
PHASES.why: Volume is now flowing, which is exactly when quality slips unnoticed. Instrumenting the guardrail before the engine scales further is what keeps the gap closed instead of merely moved.
steps: Compare new channel lead to opportunity rate against the existing baseline.
Define the minimum qualification bar new leads must clear.
Add a scoring or routing filter enforcing that bar.
Set a weekly review of new channel conversion versus baseline.
Adjust targeting on any channel that drops below the bar.
PHASES.del: A lead quality guardrail with a defined qualification bar and a weekly new versus baseline conversion review.
PHASES.li: New channel lead to opportunity rate holding within range of the existing baseline as volume grows.
PHASES.watch: Celebrating raw lead growth while conversion quietly erodes. If new channel leads convert at half the baseline, the shortage has just relocated downstream. Watch the rate, not the count.

PHASES.t: Measure qualified lead volume against the pipeline target
PHASES.dw: Qualified lead volume is shown pre and post against the pipeline target and the residual gap is quantified with a next action decided.
PHASES.hyp: The scaled sources plus the new engine closed a measurable share of the demand gap, and the next constraint is now visible.
PHASES.obj: You can show qualified lead volume before versus after against the pipeline target, attribute the lift to the engine, and name what closes the residual gap.
PHASES.why: Closing the loop is what makes this a demand system rather than a campaign. It proves the volume against the target and sets the baseline for the next cycle.
steps: Compare qualified lead volume pre versus post against the target.
Attribute the lift across scaled sources and new channels.
Measure the residual gap still open against pipeline maths.
Document which channels earned their cost and which did not.
Identify the next action to close the residual gap.
PHASES.del: A pre and post qualified lead volume report against target with attribution and a named next action.
PHASES.li: A clean, defensible volume delta that survives scrutiny from someone who did not build it.
PHASES.watch: Attributing a normal seasonal demand bump to your engine. If quarter end urgency inflated volume anyway, guard the causal claim before you bank the win.

2.q: The demand gap is small and current qualified lead volume is close to what the pipeline maths requires.
2.pass: Proceed to the source audit as planned.
2.miss: If the gap is near zero, traffic is not the constraint. The shortfall is conversion or win rate. Stop and route to a conversion diagnosis rather than building demand you do not need.

3.q: Existing scalable sources have enough headroom to close most of the gap on their own.
3.pass: Scale the known sources first and scope net new channels to the residual gap only.
3.miss: Existing sources are tapped out. Commit fully to net new channel selection in week 5 to 6 and size the test budgets to the whole gap, not a residual.

6.q: New channel leads are converting materially below the existing qualified lead baseline.
6.pass: Continue scaling the engine and proceed to final measurement.
6.miss: Stop scaling volume. The new channels are producing unqualified traffic. Tighten targeting and the qualification bar before adding spend, or the gap simply reopens at the conversion stage.

1.t: Pull win rate and average deal value
how: Export every closed won and closed lost opportunity for the last four quarters.
Win rate = closed won divided by closed won plus closed lost, calculated per quarter, never blended across the year.
Average deal value = total closed won revenue divided by closed won count.
Exclude any deal above three times the median so one outlier does not set the number.
1.need: CRM export with close date, stage and amount
1.done: Four quarterly win rates and one trimmed average deal value, both agreed with sales
1.care: A blended twelve month win rate hides seasonality and quietly flatters the gap.

1.t: Back solve the leads the target needs
how: Opportunities needed = revenue target divided by average deal value.
Qualified leads needed = opportunities needed divided by win rate.
If your qualified stage sits earlier than opportunity, divide again by the lead to opportunity rate.
State the result per month, not per quarter, so it can be tracked on a cadence people work to.
1.need: Revenue target for the period, win rate, average deal value
1.done: One required volume per month, with the method written beside it
1.care: Using the target you would like to hit rather than the one the business is held to.

1.t: Count the qualified leads you actually produce
how: Pull the last twelve months by month, using the exact stage definition from step two.
Exclude recycled records and duplicates, and say how many you removed.
Split inbound and outbound if they qualify on different criteria.
Sense check the total against the marketing source report before you use it.
1.need: Marketing source report on the same stage definition
1.done: Twelve monthly figures on one identical definition, duplicates removed
1.care: Counting MQLs against a required figure that was built on SQLs.

how: Gap = required volume minus actual volume, calculated for every one of the twelve months.
Express it as a percentage of required as well as an absolute number.
Look at the direction of travel across the twelve months, not only the latest month.
Write the single current figure at the top of the sheet in plain language.
1.need: Both figures above, on the same definition
1.done: One current gap figure plus its twelve month direction
1.care: A single month gap that a seasonal quarter fully explains.

1.t: Get sales and finance to sign it
how: Walk each of them through the method first and the number second.
Ask each one directly what would have to be true for this number to be wrong.
Log every objection in the sheet and resolve it there, in writing.
Get an explicit yes from both before anything downstream is scoped.
1.need: Draft gap calculation, thirty minutes with each function
1.done: Written agreement from sales and finance, objections logged and closed
1.care: Verbal agreement in a meeting that nobody ever puts in writing.

2.t: List every source producing qualified leads
how: Pull twelve months of qualified leads grouped by first touch source.
Roll anything under two percent of volume into a single Other line.
Name one accountable owner per source, including the ones nobody currently owns.
Flag any source where attribution is known to be unreliable rather than silently trusting it.
2.done: Every source listed once, nothing missing, no double counting
2.care: Sources that only exist in one person's head and never appear in the report.

2.t: Record volume and cost per lead for each
how: Cost per qualified lead = total source cost divided by qualified leads from that source.
Include agency retainers, tooling and content production, not media spend alone.
Apply a thirty day lag between spend and lead so the two line up.
Do it monthly for twelve months, not as one annual average.
2.need: Ad platform spend, agency invoices, CRM lead counts
2.done: Every source has a monthly volume and a fully loaded cost per qualified lead
2.care: Media only costing, which makes expensive channels look cheap.

how: Plot cost per qualified lead against monthly spend for each source across twelve months.
Find the spend level where cost per lead starts climbing rather than holding flat.
Headroom = that inflection spend minus current spend, converted into leads at current efficiency.
Where there is no inflection in the data yet, say so and cap the estimate at plus thirty percent.
2.need: Twelve months of spend against yield per source
2.done: A ceiling figure per source, in leads, with the evidence behind it
2.care: Assuming a channel scales linearly because it has never been pushed hard enough to prove otherwise.

2.t: Rank by marginal cost of one more lead
how: Marginal cost = change in spend divided by change in leads between consecutive months.
Rank sources ascending, cheapest marginal lead first.
Ignore any source with fewer than thirty leads in the period, the maths is noise below that.
Compare each against your target cost per qualified lead, not against each other alone.
2.need: Source cost table and headroom estimate
2.done: A ranked list, cheapest marginal lead first, thin sources excluded
2.care: Ranking on average cost, which rewards sources that are already saturated.

2.t: Split into scale now versus tapped out
how: Scale now if headroom is above fifteen percent and marginal cost sits under the target.
Tapped out if either test fails, and write which one and why.
Total the leads that scaling alone would add.
Subtract that from the demand gap to get the residual the new channels must cover.
2.need: The ranking and the headroom estimates
2.done: Every source in one bucket with a written reason, and a residual gap figure
2.care: Declaring a channel tapped out when the real problem is tired creative or a stale offer.

3.t: Map where the ICP already looks
how: Interview ten buyers from recently won deals, twenty minutes each.
Ask where they were looking before they found you, whose opinion they trust, and what they searched.
Tally the answers verbatim, do not summarise them into themes too early.
Any channel named fewer than three times is not evidence yet.
3.need: Ten recent won deals and their buyer contacts
3.done: A tallied list of named channels with counts, not a set of impressions
3.care: Interviewing your champions instead of the economic buyer who actually chose.

3.t: Score candidates on fit, cost and speed
how: Score each candidate one to five on ICP fit, expected cost per qualified lead, and weeks to first signal.
Double weight the fit score, because fit is what everything else depends on.
Drop anything scoring under eight out of twenty.
Write one line of evidence beside every score so it can be challenged later.
3.need: ICP channel map and your target cost per qualified lead
3.done: Every candidate scored with the evidence recorded beside it
3.care: Scoring on how easy a channel is to launch rather than how well it fits.

3.t: Size test budgets to the residual gap only
how: Take the residual gap from phase two, not the whole demand gap.
Budget = residual leads multiplied by expected cost per lead, multiplied by 1.4 for the learning period.
Cap the test at eight weeks so a bad channel cannot quietly run all quarter.
Write the kill condition and the number that triggers it before any money moves.
3.need: Residual gap figure and expected cost per lead per channel
3.done: A budget per channel, a time cap, and a written kill condition
3.care: Sizing to the full gap and paying twice for volume the existing sources would have produced.

3.t: Define the qualification bar before spending
how: Set the floor at eighty percent of the current lead to opportunity rate.
Write the firmographic and behavioural criteria a lead must meet, explicitly.
Build it into the CRM as a required check, not as guidance in a document.
Agree with sales who enforces it and what happens to a lead that fails.
3.need: Existing lead to opportunity baseline, CRM admin access
3.done: A written threshold live in the CRM with an owner attached
3.care: Defining the bar after volume starts arriving, when nobody wants to reject anything.

3.t: Commit to two channels, not five
how: Take the top two by score and stop there.
Write one paragraph per channel on why it beat the others.
Assign one owner per channel, not one owner across both.
Put the kill condition and review date in the same document.
3.done: Two named channels, written rationale, owners and kill conditions set
3.care: Hedging across five channels, which produces five under resourced tests and no signal.

how: Name the countable thing for each channel: posts, sequences, campaigns, events.
Set the number per week, and make it a number one person can genuinely produce.
Write what does not count, so the metric cannot be gamed by volume.
Start lower than feels ambitious, because missing week two kills the habit.
4.need: Selected channels and honest team capacity
4.done: One countable unit per channel with a weekly number attached
4.care: Setting a heroic cadence that survives three weeks and then collapses.

4.t: Build the production process behind it
how: Write every step from brief to live, with the name of who does it.
Set the deadline for each step so the weekly deadline is not the only one.
Build a two week buffer of finished work before you launch anything.
Decide now what gets cut first in a bad week, rather than deciding it in a bad week.
4.need: Output definition and the people who will do the work
4.done: A written runbook plus two weeks of finished work in the queue
4.care: A process that only works when the person who designed it is in the room.

4.t: Name one owner accountable for cadence
how: One name, not a team and not a committee.
Put weekly output on their objectives, in writing.
Give them the authority to stop the line when quality would slip.
Name the deputy who covers when they are away.
4.done: One named owner with cadence on their objectives and a named deputy
4.care: Shared ownership, which reliably means nobody notices the first missed week.

4.t: Ship the first two weeks live
how: Launch, do not pilot. A pilot has no deadline and produces no signal.
Publish on the day committed even when the work is only good enough.
Log everything that nearly stopped the week, while it is still fresh.
Fix the top blocker before week three rather than adding new output.
4.need: Runbook, owner, and the buffer of finished work
4.done: Two consecutive weeks shipped on the committed day, blockers logged
4.care: Slipping week one by a few days, which sets the precedent for every week after.

4.t: Track leads produced per weekly cycle
how: Tag every channel with its own UTM or source value before launch, not after.
Report weekly, not monthly, so a bad cycle is visible while it can still be fixed.
Number the cycles so trends read as a sequence rather than as dates.
Publish the same chart to the same place every week without being asked.
4.need: Attribution wired to each channel before the first send
4.done: A weekly qualified lead number per channel, visible to the whole team
4.care: Attribution added after launch, which loses the first weeks permanently.

5.t: Compare new channel conversion to baseline
how: Measure lead to opportunity rate for the new channel cohort and the existing one, same window.
Wait for at least fifty leads per channel before drawing any conclusion.
Compare like for like, same stage definitions and the same time to convert.
Show it as a rate, never as a raw count.
5.need: Lead to opportunity data for both cohorts
5.done: A like for like rate comparison with enough volume to mean something
5.care: Judging a channel at fifteen leads and killing something that was working.

5.t: Set the minimum bar a lead must clear
how: Set the floor at eighty percent of the existing baseline conversion rate.
Write the specific criteria, not the principle.
Agree it with sales before it is enforced, so rejections are not a surprise.
Set the date it gets reviewed rather than leaving it fixed forever.
5.need: Conversion comparison and the existing baseline
5.done: A written, agreed threshold with a review date
5.care: A bar set so high that it strangles a channel before it has been tuned.

5.t: Enforce it with scoring or routing
how: Add the check in the CRM so it runs on every lead automatically.
Route leads below the bar to nurture, never to a sales rep.
Log every rejection with its reason so channels can be tuned from real data.
Test it on last month's leads before it goes live on this month's.
5.need: Quality threshold and CRM admin access
5.done: Routing live, rejections logged with reasons, tested on historic data first
5.care: Silently dropping rejected leads, which destroys the data you need to fix the channel.

5.t: Review new versus baseline every week
how: Fifteen minutes, same slot every week, owner presents.
One chart only: conversion rate by channel by week.
Sales confirms lead quality from their side, not just the dashboard.
Every review ends with a decision, even if the decision is to wait one more week.
5.need: Routing live and one week of data
5.done: A standing weekly review with an owner and a decision recorded each time
5.care: A review that becomes a status update because nothing is ever decided in it.

5.t: Retune any channel that drops below
how: Change one thing at a time: targeting first, then creative, then offer.
Give each change two full weeks before judging it.
Pause any channel that sits below the bar for two consecutive weeks after a change.
Record what you changed and what happened, so the next cycle is not a fresh start.
5.need: Weekly review data and rejection reasons
5.done: Every failing channel adjusted or paused, with the change and result recorded
5.care: Changing targeting, creative and budget at once, which teaches you nothing.

6.t: Compare volume before and after against target
how: Use the exact definition from phase one, or the comparison is meaningless.
Plot six months before and the twelve weeks after on one chart.
Mark the engine launch date on the chart so the reader sees the break point.
State the before and after averages as numbers, not only as a line.
6.need: Baseline volume and current volume, same definition
6.done: One chart plus two averages, with the launch date marked
6.care: Quietly changing the lead definition partway through, which invents a win.

6.t: Attribute the lift across sources and channels
how: Split the lift by source, separating scaled existing sources from net new channels.
Name what you cannot attribute and leave it unassigned rather than distributing it.
Check whether the period contained a seasonal effect that would have happened anyway.
Show the split as a share of the total lift.
6.need: Attribution data for the full period
6.done: Every unit of lift either assigned to a source or explicitly marked unattributed
6.care: Assigning the unattributable remainder to the newest channel because it is the newest.

6.t: Measure the residual gap still open
how: Rerun the phase one calculation with current figures, same method.
If win rate or deal value moved, recalculate required volume before comparing.
Express the residual in leads and as a percentage of required.
Compare against the original gap so the progress is a number, not a feeling.
6.need: Current volume, current win rate and deal value
6.done: A residual figure calculated the same way as the original
6.care: Comparing against the old required volume after the target has already moved.

6.t: Document which channels earned their cost
how: Put cost per qualified lead against the target bar for every channel.
Put its qualification rate against the baseline in the same table.
Make an explicit keep, tune or cut call on each, with the reason.
Include the ones you scaled, not only the new ones.
6.need: Cost and yield per channel for the full period
6.done: A keep, tune or cut decision on every channel, reason written
6.care: Keeping an underperforming channel because of the effort already spent on it.

6.t: Name the next action to close the residual
how: If the residual is under fifteen percent, the next constraint is probably conversion, route there.
If it is above, commit to one more scaling cycle on the channels that earned their cost.
Assign one owner and one date, in the document.
Set the baseline for the next cycle now, while the numbers are fresh.
6.need: Residual gap, attribution breakdown and channel verdict
6.done: One named action with an owner and a date, and a baseline set for next cycle
6.care: Ending the quarter with a report instead of a decision.

IND: shrinking week over week toward zero
Qualified leads per weekly engine cycle
New channel cost per qualified lead
at or below the defined threshold
Qualified lead volume versus pipeline target
meeting required volume to hit target
New channel lead to opportunity rate
within range of the existing baseline
